content: Among individuals who inject drugs or are incarcerated, some studies were still ongoing when their results were reported. This particularly influenced the percentages of individuals who initiated treatment and were assessed for sustained virological response (SVR). For those who started treatment, the numbers provided outside square brackets represent the proportion of individuals who underwent pretreatment assessment as the denominator, which was available for some studies. In contrast, the numbers within square brackets use the RNA-positive population as the denominator and are utilized in the quantitative analysis. For example, in a study by Ustianowski (2020) involving prisoners, laboratory assays were conducted off-site, with results reported at different intervals. Similarly, in the HEADSTART Punjab study (2020), involving people living with HIV, point-of-care (PoC) assays were performed on-site, with varying interquartile ranges (IQRs) for time intervals between testing and treatment initiation. The IQRs for laboratory-based PoC assays conducted off-site were also reported, showing slightly different timeframes. Key terms used in these studies include: IQR (Interquartile Range): Ab (Antibody): Refers to the detection of antibodies. MSF (Médecins Sans Frontières): An international medical humanitarian organization. S site/D site: Indicates whether testing and treatment occurred at the same site or different sites. S visit/NS visit: Refers to whether testing and treatment occurred during the same visit or not. The model-of-care categorization relates to the location and timing of testing and treatment. For example, some models began with RNA testing or included individuals already identified as antibody-positive. In some cases, low RNA-positive percentages were attributed to models starting at RNA testing or recruiting populations previously determined to be antibody-positive. Studies where less than 50% of antibody-positive patients were RNA-positive were primarily among people who inject drugs or prisoners. Reflex testing, a strategy to simplify access to hepatitis C virus (HCV) viral load testing, was evaluated in this systematic review. Reflex testing involves automatically performing a viral load test following a positive HCV antibody test, without requiring additional visits or sample collection. Two main types of reflex testing were identified: 1. Laboratory-based reflex testing: A single blood sample is collected and sent to a laboratory. If the antibody test is positive, the same sample is used for viral load testing. 2. Clinic-based reflex testing: A rapid diagnostic antibody test is performed on-site, followed by immediate blood collection for viral load testing if the antibody test is positive. The review found that reflex testing significantly reduced turnaround times from screening to viral load testing and improved linkage to care and treatment initiation compared to conventional multi-step testing strategies. Laboratory-based reflex testing achieved a 96% uptake of RNA testing among antibody-positive individuals, with 58% diagnosed with HCV infection and 45% initiating treatment. In comparison, non-reflex testing had lower uptake rates and longer turnaround times. Clinic-based reflex testing also demonstrated high uptake rates, with 94% of antibody-positive individuals initiating RNA testing and 84% starting treatment. Turnaround times for clinic-based reflex testing were often reduced to zero days for RNA sample collection and testing. Overall, reflex testing, whether laboratoryor clinic-based, was shown to be feasible and effective in diverse settings, including resource-limited environments. It has the potential to improve outcomes across the HCV care continuum by increasing testing uptake, reducing delays, and facilitating prompt treatment initiation. These findings support the adoption of reflex testing as an alternative to conventional multi-step diagnostic strategies to enhance HCV care and treatment globally.
